NoisyCLIP read through a small network

This page reads the whole method one idea at a time, using a network of 8 latent numbers you can check by hand. It is the place to start, and every other rung of the ladder is linked from the idea it helps with.

The question behind it. Paper 2 needs five abstract scores on a half-drawn picture, such as whether a cat is to the left of a dog. This ladder explains a cheaper candidate: score the half-drawn latent against one right sentence and one wrong sentence, and use the difference as the checker.

What is established and what is not. NoisyCLIP's published results rank seeds by this kind of score, and the paper never pushes a sampler with it. No result on this project's pictures exists yet. Whether it reads or steers any of the five properties is what steps W2 and W3 will measure. Numbers marked "toy" come from the miniature, whose weights are set by hand and predict nothing about SDXL.

1. A half-drawn latent gets a rough colour view

CLIP reads colour pictures and SDXL's latent has 4 channels, so a fixed table turns the 4 channels into red, green and blue without running the VAE decoder.

redR​​=a fixed weighted sum60z0​−60z1​+25z2​−70z3​​​+bias150​​

On the toy. Pixel A has channels (1,0.5,0,0.5), so its red is 60−30+0−35+150=145. Work all six colours.

2. The clamp and the byte conversion block the signal

The released code holds each colour between 0 and 255 and then converts it to 8-bit integers. A held colour passes no gradient, and the conversion passes none at all.

On unit-variance noise the clamp holds 26.8% of red, 11.4% of green and 7.0% of blue values, computed from the weights with independent channels. A half-drawn SDXL latent has structure, so its share has to be measured.

On the toy. Pixel B's red is 305, so it is held at 255 and sends nothing back. See the four ways the signal dies.

3. Only the image encoder learned to read noise

NoisyCLIP is CLIP ViT-L/14 with its image encoder fine-tuned on noisy SDXL latents, and its text side left alone so the sentence vectors keep their meaning.

L=21​[each latent picks its captionCE(ets​s, rows)​​+each caption picks its latentCE(ets​s, columns)​​]

The published weights match base CLIP exactly on both projection heads and on the first text layer, and differ by 6.1% of its norm on the first vision layer. Only those tensors were compared. The released --only_vision flag would leave the image projection trainable, while the published weights show it unchanged.

On the toy. One update of the image layer takes the loss from 0.9264 to 0.7929 and leaves the sentence vectors where they were. Work the training step.

4. It practised on later steps than this loop would push

The paper trains on latents 20 to 29 of a 50-step run (p. 6). This loop reads steps 0 to 15, which are noisier and outside that window, and W3 pushes only on the steps in that range that W2 can read.

At step 0 the signal scale is 0.076, at step 15 it is 0.3076, and at step 20 it is 0.4241 (computed from SDXL's scheduler config). The paper's own measures at these early latents are on its own captions: it marks separation at latent 10 (p. 10), where the right caption's Recall@1 is about 0.20, which is chance among five captions (Fig. 4, as read in the reading note). Its Recall@1, the share of images whose right caption ranks first of 5, is 0.506 over latents 21 to 30 against 0.145 for frozen CLIP (p. 14).

5. Two sentences turn a score into a checker

The same picture is scored against a right sentence and a wrong one, and the difference is the checker's output.

D=Sright​I⋅Tright​​​−Swrong​I⋅Twrong​​​=I⋅where the sentences differ(Tright​−Twrong​)​​

The pair "a cat to the left of a dog" and "a dog to the left of a cat" uses the same words, so this checker depends on the text encoder giving the two orders different vectors.

On the toy. D=0.9687−0.9995=−0.0308, so the toy picture starts closer to the wrong sentence.

Can the text side tell the two orders apart? A text-only check answers this before any image is read. If a sentence vector were a sum of one vector per word slot, averaging both word orders would cancel the swap exactly.

What survives the averaging is 0.72 of the colour-binding swap in trained CLIP, against 0.13 with random weights, and 0.28 of the left-right swap, against 0.08. So the text side carries binding and carries order weakly (the W2 review's word check). This check reads no image and says nothing about NoisyCLIP's image side.

6. The gradient walks back to the latent

The chain rule carries the score difference back through every step, and each of the latent's numbers receives its share.

g=∇xt​​[Sright​−Swrong​]

This g is a classifier's gradient up to size. Treating the two sentences as two classes gives ∇logp(right)=(1−p)ets​g, so the push has classifier guidance's direction, and a fixed λ replaces a factor that would shrink as the classifier grows confident. The companion derives this.

On the toy. The entry of g largest in size is −0.1149, on pixel A's channel z1​. Work the backward pass.

7. The push changes the noise prediction

The gradient is taken at the latent, and the correction goes onto the noise prediction the sampler is about to use.

ϵ^t​=product or CO3ϵbase​​​−strengthλ​​noise levelσt​​​g∇xt​​[Sright​−Swrong​]​​

On the toy. With λ=2 and σt​=0.8, one DDIM step ends at a score difference of −0.0791 with the push and −0.0984 without it. Work the step. A hand-set network moving in the push's direction says nothing about whether a real picture would.

8. What would make it fail

These are the failure routes the wiring allows. Each is a question for W2 or W3, and none has been measured here.

The text side barely tells the two orders apart. Identical vectors would give a zero difference and a zero push. The text-only word check finds 0.28 of the left-right swap surviving, so the order checker has a small target (section 5).

The score moves and the picture does not. A CLIP checker on the decoded image raised its own score and did not move where the animals were (the checker loop), so a score that rises is not evidence on its own.

The steps are outside the training window. The model practised on steps 20 to 29 and this loop would use steps 0 to 15.

The clamp removes part of the direction the push needs. In the toy, pixel B's red would send back 0.2154 and the clamp sends back 0.

9. The paper's notation

The paper writes the latent as zt​, the text encoder as τθ​, the image encoder as νθ​ and the path into RGB as Φ. Its score (p. 5) is

Slatent​(zt​,y)=τθ​(y)⋅νθ​(Φ(zt​)).

In this ladder's symbols that is S=T⋅I, with T=τθ​(y) and I=νθ​(Φ(xt​)). The paper uses this score to choose which seeds keep running, and its gradient appears nowhere in the paper. The notation table maps every symbol.

The network view: what NoisyCLIP adds to CLIP

These figures open the sentence-score push into the network it is, with real sizes from CLIP ViT-L/14's public config. CLIP's own insides are already drawn on the CLIP ladder, so each of its figures is linked at the point it helps and only what NoisyCLIP adds is drawn here.

Reading the colours. Lilac is text, green is image, pale blue is a matching pair, orange is the push and grey is frozen or fixed. The linked CLIP figures keep their own key, where orange marks the shared space and the loss.

No result on this project's pictures exists yet. These figures show how the method is wired. Whether it reads or steers any of the five properties is what steps W2 and W3 will measure.

The whole picture

1. The same two encoders do three jobs

The model is trained once on a contrastive loss, then read and pushed with its weights held. Open this first when you lose track of which job a later figure belongs to.

2. The read and push path, with every size

The orange lane ends at xt​ because that is where the gradient is read. The result then joins ϵbase​, so nothing is added to the latent directly.

Linked from the CLIP ladder. The whole of CLIP shows the two towers on ViT-B/32, and the module tree opens every layer.

The path into the image encoder

3. Four latent channels become three colours

Each colour is a fixed weighted sum of the four channels, with no VAE decoder. The tiles are synthetic Gaussian noise pushed through the real weights.

4. The clamp stops the gradient

The left plot has the map's value on x and the clamped value on y, both in RGB units. The right plot shows the share of pixels clamped on unit-variance noise, computed from the weights with independent channels: 26.8% of red, 11.4% of green and 7.0% of blue.

5. What is tuned and what is frozen

The published weights change the image encoder. Both projection heads and the first text layer equal base CLIP exactly, and the first vision layer differs by 6.1% of its norm (the checkpoint comparison). Only those tensors were compared. The released --only_vision flag would leave the image projection trainable, while the published weights show it unchanged.

Linked from the CLIP ladder. The picture's path walks the patch cut and tokens, and one query asking the keys opens attention.

Training on noisy latents

6. Training pulls each latent toward its caption

The matrix cells are labelled by their product and hold no values. The CLIP ladder's four pictures against four captions and its two softmaxes show the same loss with real scores.

7. Which noise levels it practised on

The x axis is the sampler step of 50 and the y axis is the scale from 0 to 1, computed from SDXL's scheduler config. The paper trains on latents 20 to 29 (p. 6), and this loop reads steps 0 to 15, which the model did not train on. W3 pushes only on the steps in that range that W2 can read.

The score and the push

8. Right minus wrong

The two sentences use the same words in a different order. The score difference depends only on the gap between their two vectors, so a text encoder that gave them the same vector would give the push nothing to follow. The circle is a two-dimensional sketch of 768-number vectors.

9. The gradient walks back to the latent

The released map blocks the gradient twice, at any clamped colour and at .byte(). The push needs a copy of the map without .byte().

10. How the push joins CO3

Our existing push code subtracts the push from both entries of CO3's main prediction, which lowers the guided prediction by exactly the push.

The text-only word check

These two figures ask whether the frozen text side can tell the two sentences of a checker apart at all, before any image is read. They are drawn in the merged style, so they carry stage brackets and result bars.

11. Average both word orders, and keep what survives

If a sentence vector were a sum of one vector per word slot, the two sums would be equal and w would be zero. The ratio ∥w∥/(2∥u1​−u3​∥) runs from 0 for a pure sum of word slots to 1 when the whole swap survives. For cat and dog it is 0.33 for order and 0.61 for colour binding, against 0.08 and 0.11 for the same encoder with random weights (the word check's numbers).

12. What survives for six noun pairs

The x axis is the ratio and each dot is one of six noun pairs. Binding averages 0.72 (0.48 to 0.94) in trained CLIP against 0.13 with random weights. Order averages 0.28 (0.22 to 0.33) against 0.08. Swapping the nouns moves a sentence 0.19 to 0.34, against 0.63 to 0.87 for changing one noun.

What this can and cannot say. It uses no image, so it bounds what any reader with this text encoder can do and says nothing about NoisyCLIP's image side. The summary and its caveats are in the W2 review's word check section.

The six illustrations

These pictures tell the idea before the sizes and the maths. Every tile in them is an image model's teaching drawing, so none is an SDXL sample and none shows a result. Their prompts and faithfulness notes are in the illustrated map.

1. A cheap colour view of the latent

A half-drawn latent is not a picture, so a fixed sum of its four channels makes a rough colour view with no decoder.

2. One picture against two sentences

The checker asks the same noisy picture about two sentences with the same words in a different order, and keeps the difference. The numbers are the miniature's.

3. Training on half-drawn pictures

Only the image side learns. Each half-drawn picture is pulled toward its own caption and away from the others.

4. The push bends the noise prediction

The gradient is taken at the latent, and what changes is the noise prediction the sampler is about to use.

5. Two places the signal is cut

The released map blocks the gradient at the conversion to bytes and at any clamped colour.

6. Trained later than this loop would push

NoisyCLIP practised on the middle of the sampling run, and this loop would use it earlier, on noisier latents.

The miniature: the whole method on 2 pixels

This is the sentence-score push small enough to do on paper. The latent has 8 numbers, the linear map is NoisyCLIP's real one, and every other weight is set by hand so each step can be checked.

This toy predicts nothing about SDXL. Its image layer was never trained on data, so a number here shows what a part computes and says nothing about whether NoisyCLIP reads or steers a real picture. Every value comes from the answer key, written by the script.

Words this uses

Pixel A, pixel B. The two positions of the toy latent, each with 4 channels.

Clamped. A colour outside 0 to 255 that the map holds at the edge, so it passes no gradient.

Image layer. A hand-set 2×6 table M that stands in for the whole 24-block ViT.

1. See the whole thing

Trace one path with your finger: the top latent number, into red, into the first hidden number, into the two scores. The picture's job is to show that each number on the later pages sits on one of these circles.

2. Work the linear map

Write out pixel A's red: 60(1)−60(0.5)+25(0)−70(0.5)+150=145. That is the first green circle in the colour column.

How it fails. Pixel B's red comes to 305, so the clamp holds it at 255 and that colour stops carrying a gradient. How you know it worked. Your six values match the "before clamp" column.

3. Work forward to the score difference

Scale each colour with p=c/255−0.5, apply the layer, divide by the length and take the two dot products:

h=(0.6373, 0.7941),I=(0.6259, 0.7799),D=0.9687−0.9995=−0.0308.

The toy starts closer to the wrong sentence, so the difference is negative. How you know it worked. Your I has length 1 and your D matches.

4. Work the gradient back

Differentiating a unit vector removes the part along itself, so with ΔT=Tright​−Twrong​:

∂h∂D​=∥h∥ΔT−(ΔT⋅I)I​=(0.2154, −0.1728).

Then multiply by M⊤, zero any clamped colour, and multiply by W/255 to reach the 8 latent numbers.

How it fails. Forgetting the clamp mask gives pixel B a share through red that the real gradient does not have. How you know it worked. Your 8 values match the table, which the script checks against automatic differentiation and against finite differences.

5. See why this is a classifier's gradient

Treat the two sentences as a two-class classifier with score multiplier ets​. Its log-probability of the right sentence has the gradient

∇xt​​logp(right∣xt​)=(1−p(right∣xt​))ets​∇xt​​[Sright​−Swrong​].

In the toy, with a multiplier of 10, p(right)=0.4236 and the factor is 5.7643, and the script confirms the identity to rounding error. So the push has classifier guidance's direction, and its fixed λ stands in for a factor that would otherwise shrink as the classifier grows confident.

6. Join the noise prediction and step

The push is λσt​g with λ=2 and σt​=0.8. Subtract it from ϵbase​, then run one DDIM step with signal scale 0.6 going to 0.8. In this step the coefficient on ϵ^t​ is −0.4667, so subtracting the push adds 0.4667p to the next latent.

The bars plot the toy's score difference after that step: −0.0984 with no push and −0.0791 with it. What this shows. The mechanics move the score in the push's direction on a hand-set network, and it is the only thing they show.

7. Break it four ways

Byte conversion. 127.9 becomes 127 and the result has no gradient, so the push path must leave it out.

The same vector for both sentences. The difference and every gradient are 0.

All three colours clamped. Setting pixel B to (3,−3,0,−3) gives colours 720, 485 and 385, and its whole gradient row is 0.

Hard clamp against soft clamp. At pixel B's red, a soft clamp of sharpness 0.05 keeps a slope of 0.0759, so its z0​ gradient is −0.0288 against −0.0407 for the hard clamp. The soft clamp also changes every other value, which is why W3 records the choice before pushing any picture.

8. One training step

The two latents are the same two pixels in swapped order, each paired with its own sentence. One gradient step of size 0.5 on M takes the loss from 0.9264 to 0.7929. The sentence vectors do not move, because the text side is frozen.

9. Work the word check on a toy

This second toy explains the text-only word check. Its sentence vectors are hand-set sums of 3-number word-slot vectors from the word check toy's key, and they are not made unit length.

Add the slot vectors for each sentence. "a cat to the left of a dog" is (2,1,0)+(0,0,1)+(0,2,1)=(2,3,2). Both pairs sum to (4,4,5), because every word slot appears once on each side, so w=(0,0,0).

Now add one term that depends on which noun sits on which side, c×side×(nfirst​−nsecond​) with c=0.5. The sums become (5,3,5) and (3,5,5), so w=(2,−2,0), which is 4c(ncat​−ndog​). The toy's ratio is 0.47.

What the toy explains. Only a term like this one can make w non-zero. Trained CLIP's ratios for cat and dog, 0.33 for order and 0.61 for binding, say its text side carries some such term. The random-weights encoder's 0.08 and 0.11 say an untrained encoder of the same shape mostly does not.

How to rerun this, and what is simplified 
cd /home/molef/PhD/concept-composition/2-classifier-guidance/artifacts/scenes/noisyclip-sentence-score/2-miniature
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES= PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 uv run --no-project --with torch python miniature.py
PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python3 word_check_toy.py
PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python3 make_miniature_figures.py

The first command stops with an assertion error if the hand chain rule, finite differences or the classifier identity disagree. The third stops if the pure sum of word slots does not cancel. The last ends with all written 0 for all nine figures.

Simplified on purpose. The resize and CLIP's normalisation are left out, the 24-block ViT is one linear layer, and the score multiplier in training is 10 where real NoisyCLIP uses 98.86.

What each line of NoisyCLIP's released code computes

This walk reads the released code block by block and ties each block to its equation and to its part of the read and push picture. It exists so a later session can write the differentiable input path for W2 and W3 without guessing what the authors' path does.

The code is novasearch/noisyclip at commit 016b91356a43e455542fd018bc16ea3b419779d2. It was read and never run. Every quoted block is checked against the file by the quote check.

1. Catching the half-drawn latents

A forward hook on the U-Net saves its first input on every call, so one 50-step image gives 50 saved tensors. This is the "noisy latent" box at the far left of every picture.

src/generate_latents.py, lines 41 to 42:

    def hook(self, module, input, output):
        self.temp_latents.append(input[0].detach().cpu())

src/generate_latents.py, lines 75 to 84:

            unet = self.pipeline.unet
            hook_handle = unet.register_forward_hook(self.hook)

            # Generate image
            image = self.pipeline(prompt, generator=generator, eta=1 if self.ddpm else 0).images[0]

            hook_handle.remove()
            save_image(image, image_path=image_path)
            save_latents(self.temp_latents, latent_path=latent_path)
            self.temp_latents = []

What the saved tensor is. The pipeline scales the Euler latent before the U-Net sees it, so the hook saves

σEuler2​+1​zt​​=αˉt​​z0​+1−αˉt​​ε.

That is the same scale as our DDIM latent xt​. The default scheduler in SDXL's scheduler config is EulerDiscreteScheduler with leading spacing, so step k of 50 uses timestep 981−20k, as our DDIM steps do.

How it fails. A raw Euler latent has a standard deviation near σEuler​ (13.12 at step 0 and 3.09 at step 15, from this ladder's numbers file). Passing it to the linear map without the scaling would saturate almost every pixel. How you know it worked. W2's first check compares this path with the authors' on 16 latents and needs a mean cosine of at least 0.99.

2. Four channels become three colours

Each colour is a fixed weighted sum of the four channels at the same position, plus a bias. No VAE decoder runs. This is the grey "linear map" box.

src/latent_to_image.py, lines 9 to 17:

def latents_to_rgb(latents):
    weights = (
        (60, -60, 25, -70),
        (60, -5, 15, -50),
        (60, 10, -5, -35)
    )
    weights_tensor = torch.t(torch.tensor(weights, dtype=latents.dtype).to(latents.device))
    biases_tensor = torch.tensor((150, 140, 130), dtype=latents.dtype).to(latents.device)
    rgb_tensor = torch.einsum("...lxy,lr -> ...rxy", latents, weights_tensor) + biases_tensor.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1)

​RGB​​=​606060​−60−510​2515−5​−70−50−35​​​z0​z1​z2​z3​​​+​150140130​​

torch.t flips the table to 4 by 3 so the einsum can sum over the latent channel l and leave the colour r. The miniature's table works this sum on two pixels.

3. The clamp and the byte conversion

src/latent_to_image.py, lines 18 to 20:

    image_array = rgb_tensor.clamp(0, 255)[0].byte().cpu().numpy()
    image_array = image_array.transpose(1, 2, 0)  # Rearrange dimensions for image
    return Image.fromarray(image_array)

Line 18 does three things. clamp(0, 255) holds each value inside the byte range, [0] takes the first of the two identical classifier-free guidance copies, and .byte() converts to 8-bit integers by dropping the decimals, so 127.9 becomes 127.

How it fails for a push. .byte() has no gradient at all, and a clamped value passes zero. On unit-variance noise the clamp holds 26.8% of red, 11.4% of green and 7.0% of blue values, and 29.5% of pixels have at least one colour clamped (the numbers file, computed from the weights with independent channels). What the push path changes. It keeps the sum and the clamp and drops .byte(). W3's design records whether the clamp stays hard or becomes soft, before any picture is pushed.

4. Which parameters train

src/train_model_classic.py, lines 47 to 51:

    elif only_vision:
        for name, param in model.named_parameters():
            param.requires_grad = not ("text" in name)
        if hasattr(model, "logit_scale"):
            model.logit_scale.requires_grad = False

src/train_model_classic.py, line 71:

    model.logit_scale.requires_grad = False

The test on line 49 is a substring test on the parameter's name. text_model.* and text_projection.* contain "text" and freeze. vision_model.* and visual_projection.weight do not, so this flag would leave the image projection trainable.

The published weights show that head unchanged. Against openai/clip-vit-large-patch14, visual_projection.weight, text_projection.weight and the first text layer's key projection have a largest absolute difference of 0, and the first vision layer's key projection differs by 6.1% of its norm (the checkpoint comparison). Only those tensors were compared, so the other text layers are stated frozen on the paper's word (p. 6) and were not checked. The command that produced the checkpoint is not released.

logit_scale is 4.59375 in the published weights and 4.60517 in base CLIP, which multiplies a score by 98.86 and 100.00.

5. The batch and the loss

src/train_model_classic.py, lines 14 to 20:

def collate_fn_standard_clip(batch):
    return {
        "pixel_values": torch.stack([b["pixel_values"] for b in batch]),
        "input_ids": torch.stack([b["input_ids"] for b in batch]),
        "attention_mask": torch.stack([b["attention_mask"] for b in batch]),
        "return_loss": True
    }

src/train_model_classic.py, lines 265 to 273:

    trainer = trainer_class(
        model=model,
        args=training_args,
        train_dataset=dataset_train,
        eval_dataset=dataset_test,
        data_collator=collate_fn,
    )
    print("Starting training...")
    trainer.train()

return_loss: True makes Hugging Face's CLIPModel compute its own contrastive loss, so the script holds no loss code. With sij​ the cosine of picture i and caption j and et the score multiplier:

L=21​[CE(ets, rows)+CE(ets, columns)]

Each picture's right answer is its own caption, and every other caption in the batch is a wrong one. The CLIP ladder's two softmaxes draws this loss with real scores.

7. What the release leaves out

The resize and normalisation. Training reads ready-made pixel_values from a preprocessed dataset, and AutoProcessor is imported and never called.

src/train_model_classic.py, lines 180 to 181:

    ds_preprocessed = load_from_disk(preprocessed_dataset_dir)
    dataset_train = ds_preprocessed["train"].with_format("torch")

W2's design takes these steps from the base model's preprocessor config: bicubic resize from 128 to 224, then CLIP's mean and standard deviation. The published checkpoint ships no processor file, so this is an inferred match that W2's first check tests.

The choice of noise levels. The script adds no noise and picks no step. The window of latents 20 to 29 exists in the paper (p. 6) and in a dataset that is not released.

A line that stops the script. Line 1 of train_model_classic.py is the bare word python, which raises a NameError if the file is run as released (inferred, since it was not run).

8. Where a push enters our sampler

This block is our code at 2-classifier-guidance/scripts/method_search/co3_push.py. It already adds a checker's push to CO3, and a sentence score would replace the checker. No sentence score has been run through it.

co3_push.py, lines 30 to 36:

    def forward(self, sample, timestep, *args, **kwargs):
        out = self.inner(sample, timestep, *args, **kwargs)
        if self.pusher is None or sample.shape[0] != 2:
            return out
        eps = out["sample"]
        push = self.pusher(sample[:1], timestep, eps).to(device=eps.device, dtype=eps.dtype)
        return UNet2DConditionOutput(sample=eps - push)

co3_push.py, lines 62 to 76:

        with torch.enable_grad():
            z = x.detach().float().requires_grad_(True)
            log_p = self.checker.log_prob_both(z, timestep.reshape(1).to(x.device))
            grad = torch.autograd.grad(log_p, z)[0]
        sigma = (1.0 - self.alpha_bar) ** 0.5
        strength = 0.0 if self.mode == "zero" else self.strength
        raw = strength * sigma * grad
        uncond, cond = eps[:1].float(), eps[1:2].float()
        limit = self.cap * (uncond + self.guidance * (cond - uncond)).norm()
        raw_norm = raw.norm()
        fired = bool(raw_norm > limit)
        push = raw * (limit / raw_norm) if fired else raw
        self.applied.append(float(push.norm()))
        self.capped.append(fired)
        return push

The gradient is taken at the latent on line 65 and multiplied by the strength and the noise level on line 68, and lines 70 to 73 cap its length. forward subtracts the result from both entries of CO3's two-entry prediction, which lowers the guided prediction by exactly the push:

(ϵu​−p)+w[(ϵc​−p)−(ϵu​−p)]=ϵu​+w(ϵc​−ϵu​)−p.

What a sentence-score version must supply. A differentiable S right minus S wrong in place of log_prob_both, a choice of cosine or scaled logit (the scale multiplies the gradient by 98.86), and a clamp rule. Those choices belong to W3's design.

Rebuild the sentence-score push from fundamentals

This page takes each equation the push depends on down to a rung the learning tree already teaches, in the order you would rebuild it. CLIP's own insides have their own rebuild and classifier guidance has another, so this page links their rungs and writes only what NoisyCLIP adds.

Table of contents

  1. The noisy latent
  2. The fixed linear map
  3. The clamp and how many pixels it holds
  4. The image encoder and its unit vector
  5. The contrastive loss with one side frozen
  6. The score difference is a two-sentence classifier
  7. The gradient of a cosine
  8. From a gradient to a noise prediction

  • Gaps

1. The noisy latent

xt​=αˉt​​x0​+1−αˉt​​ε

What the code does. The released hook saves the U-Net's scaled input, which is this quantity (block 1 of the code walk).

Where it is taught. The schedule and forward noising works it on a small network, and the forward process by hand builds αˉ from SDXL's scaled-linear betas.

2. The fixed linear map

c=Wz+b

Rung 1: a matrix times a vector is one weighted sum per row

Red is row one of W dotted with the four channels, plus its bias. On pixel A of the miniature, 60(1)−60(0.5)+25(0)−70(0.5)+150=145.

Where it is taught. The linear map card lists the textbook pages and videos.

Rung 2: the gradient of a linear map is its transpose

If c=Wz+b, a gradient u on c becomes W⊤u on z. So each latent channel collects its colours' gradients, each weighted by the number that connected them.

Where it is taught. The backpropagation card, and the chain rule run back into the input.

3. The clamp and how many pixels it holds

clamp(c)=min(max(c,0),255),dcdclamp​={10​0<c<255otherwise​

Rung 3: a flat function has no slope to pass back

The clamp is flat outside its range, the same way a ReLU is flat below zero. Understanding deep learning, page 52 names that zero derivative, and Probabilistic machine learning, page 495 names the "dead ReLU" it causes.

Rung 4: a weighted sum of independent unit Gaussians is Gaussian

Red's standard deviation is 602+602+252+702​=112.81, around a mean of 150. The share clamped is the area of that bell below 0 and above 255:

Φ(112.81−150​)+Φ(112.81150−255​)=9.2%+17.6%=26.8%.

Where it is taught. Probabilistic machine learning, page 67 covers the variance of a scaled variable, and Pattern classification, page 720 covers the area under a Gaussian.

The limit of this number. It assumes independent unit-variance channels, which holds for pure noise. A half-drawn SDXL latent has structure, so its clamped share has to be measured.

4. The image encoder and its unit vector

I=∥projection(ViT(Φ(xt​)))∥projection(ViT(Φ(xt​)))​

Where it is taught. The CLIP rebuild walks the vision tower from its parameters to its output. NoisyCLIP changes the weights of this tower and keeps its shape.

5. The contrastive loss with one side frozen

L=21​[CE(ets​s, rows)+CE(ets​s, columns)]

What is new. Only the image side receives the update. In the miniature's training step, the loss falls and the sentence vectors stay where they were, so the image encoder learns to place noisy latents near a text space that never moves.

Where it is taught. CLIP's dot product as a cosine and the CLIP chapter on one small network.

6. The score difference is a two-sentence classifier

Rung 5: a two-way softmax has a one-line gradient

Let a=ets​Sright​ and b=ets​Swrong​. Then logp(right)=a−log(ea+eb), and differentiating gives

∇logp(right)=(1−p(right))∇(a−b)=(1−p(right))ets​∇[Sright​−Swrong​].

So the push's direction is a classifier's gradient. Its size differs, because the factor (1−p)ets​ shrinks as the classifier grows confident and a fixed λ does not.

Where it is taught. The classifier's slope is one minus its probability is the same identity for a cat and dog classifier. The miniature checks it to rounding error.

7. The gradient of a cosine

Rung 6: differentiating a unit vector removes the part along itself

For I=h/∥h∥ and a fixed vector u,

∂h∂(I⋅u)​=∥h∥u−(u⋅I)I​.

The gradient is perpendicular to I, so it turns the embedding and cannot lengthen it. With u=ΔT, this is the first card of the miniature's backward pass.

Where it is taught. The cosine similarity card teaches the cosine. This derivative is listed under Gaps.

8. From a gradient to a noise prediction

ϵ^t​=ϵbase​−λσt​∇xt​​[Sright​−Swrong​]

Why σt​ appears. A noise prediction is minus the noise level times the score, so a change to the score becomes −σt​ times that change in the noise prediction.

Where it is taught. Noise prediction is minus the noise level times the score, and Algorithm 2 takes the push off the noise prediction.

9. The DDIM step

xt−1​=αˉt−1​​αˉt​​xt​−σt​ϵ^t​​+σt−1​ϵ^t​

Where it is taught. The DDIM update and the DDIM card.

The order to rebuild it

  1. Noise one toy latent with the schedule (section 1).
  2. Write the linear map and its transpose (section 2).
  3. Add the clamp and count the pixels it holds (section 3).
  4. Write the unit vector and the cosine gradient (sections 4 and 7).
  5. Build the score difference and check the two-sentence identity (section 6).
  6. Join the push to a noise prediction and run one DDIM step (sections 8 and 9).
  7. Train one contrastive step with the text side frozen (section 5).

The miniature's script is this order in about 150 lines.

Gaps

The gradient of a cosine with respect to its input. No page in the learning tree derives ∂(I⋅u)/∂h. Section 7 holds the derivation, and a short textbook section would fill the gap.

A soft clamp's trade-off. Nothing in the tree compares a hard clamp with a smooth one for guidance. The miniature's fourth break shows the mechanics on two pixels only.

Bicubic resize as a linear operator. The push passes back through a resize from 128 to 224, and no page teaches the transpose of that resampling.

NoisyCLIP as a sentence-score push: a zoom ladder

This ladder explains one candidate for Paper 2's abstract checkers: a noise-aware CLIP reads a half-drawn SDXL latent, scores it against a right and a wrong sentence, and the gradient of the difference pushes the sampler. It climbs from the whole sampler down to a network of 8 latent numbers.

Open noisyclip-ladder.html first. It is one self-contained page holding every rung. The same content is in the markdown files below.

What is established and what is proposed

NoisyCLIP's results are the paper's own. It ranks seeds during sampling and reports its numbers on its own benchmarks. It never feeds a gradient to a sampler.

The push is our proposal. No result on this project's pictures exists yet. Steps W2 and W3 measure whether it reads or steers any of the five properties.

The miniature is a toy. Its weights are set by hand, so it shows what each part computes and predicts nothing about SDXL.

How it was made

The sizes come from the public configs of openai/clip-vit-large-patch14 and SDXL's scheduler, and the parameter counts come from building that config on PyTorch's meta device, with no weights. The released code was read at commit 016b913 and never run. The checkpoint itself was not downloaded here, and the facts about its weights come from the checkpoint comparison. The illustrations were drawn by Codex's image tool from prompts built on the miniature's numbers, so every tile in them is a teaching drawing and none is an SDXL sample.
